context: Round 2 has Squire start and keep its own Claude Code session: one session, reachable from the Claude app on the Mac and on the phone, back by itself after a restart, a crash or sleep, under the Squire owner's own Claude sign-in and never an API key. Round 1 proved the floor by passing core's settings with --settings; claude remote-control refuses that flag, and its sessions read the project and local settings of the folder they run in, where a settings file holding disableAllHooks switches every hook off mid-session. Claude Code also has its own permission prompts, a second approval channel beside the floor. Wake-ups the Squire owner picks must reach only Squire's own session and send nothing when Squire is unsure, and a wake-up's text must never count as the Squire owner's yes. Every runtime fact below was measured on 2026-11-08 on a test user's Mac with Claude Code 2.1.319 through the entry points named here, unless a documentation page is named (code.claude.com: remote-control, cross-session messaging, hooks, settings, CLI reference) or the fact is marked owed.
decision:
1. Entry points, by path, each run by /usr/bin/python3 -B from the installed core in the Squire home: the session runner core/tools/runner.py; the wake-up router core/tools/wake-up.py (wake-up.py <text> delivers one wake-up now; wake-up.py --due delivers the Squire owner's picked wake-ups (wakeUps in the Squire owner's squire.json, each "HH:MM text" in the Mac's local time) that have come due and not gone today, once a day each, and the retries now due; how late a picked wake-up missed while the Mac slept may still go is a question for the Squire owner); the SessionStart hook core/hooks/session-start.py and the ConfigChange hook core/hooks/config-change.py, wired in core/settings.json beside the PreToolUse and UserPromptSubmit hooks, as command hooks run by /usr/bin/python3 from ${SQUIRE_HOME}/core; the health check core/tools/health.py (exit 0 and no output when healthy, a health line per problem otherwise); lay-down core/tools/lay-down.py.
2. The two launchd agents. Lay-down writes them into Library/LaunchAgents under the home folder it is given, each file named for its label, each running /usr/bin/python3 with the installed copies under the Squire home and SQUIRE_HOME in its environment: the runner (RunAtLoad and KeepAlive) and the wake-up scheduler (wake-up.py --due every 60 seconds, StartInterval). Lay-down loads them into the Squire owner's login session only when the home folder it writes into is the account's own home folder, as the account database names it: launchd reads that folder at login and no other, and a test world, whose home is a temporary folder, reaches no real launchd domain. The real load is proven on a target Mac only.
3. The config folder. Claude Code's config folder for Squire's session is claude-config in the Squire home, so the session never reads the Squire owner's ~/.claude/settings*.json. Lay-down writes its settings.json from core's settings each time it lays core down. Before each start the runner writes its .claude.json answering "trust this folder" for the Squire owner's folder (projects.<folder>.hasTrustDialogAccepted) and "Enable Remote Control" (remoteDialogSeen) in advance, keeping everything else Claude Code keeps there, the sign-in record among it. The folder has its own Keychain sign-in item: the Squire owner signs in once with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR set to it; the runner never signs in and never opens a sign-in.
4. The environment, built from nothing whatever the runner's own environment holds: PATH /usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin, then the folder of the claude the runner runs, then /opt/homebrew/bin; HOME, as given; USER, the name of the user the runner runs as, from the account database (without it claude auth status answered not signed in from the same folder); SQUIRE_HOME; CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR; LANG, a UTF-8 locale. Never ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (a key bills beyond the plan), and never CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS.
5. The claude it runs, where ~ is the HOME the runner is given (launchd gives the account's own): ~/.local/bin/claude, then /usr/local/bin/claude, then /opt/homebrew/bin/claude, the first whose file (a link's target, as Claude Code's installer lays one) is owned by the user Squire runs as and is not writable by others; never a PATH lookup. With none, no session starts and the health check says so.
6. The check before each start. No session starts, the runner exits non-zero (its agent runs it again) and the health check names what is wrong, when: core's installed settings.json or any of the four floor hooks (pre-tool-use.py, user-prompt-submit.py, session-start.py, config-change.py) is missing; the config folder's settings.json is missing or differs from core's installed settings, compared as parsed JSON; no claude can be trusted (line 5); or claude auth status, run in the session's environment, does not answer signed in (never a sign-in window, never a Terminal).
7. The server: in the Squire owner's folder, claude remote-control --spawn session --permission-mode bypassPermissions --name <squireName from the Squire owner's squire.json, "Squire" when it has none>, started as the leader of its own process group, its output appended to logs/session.log in the Squire home. Never --fork-session, --continue, --session-id, --settings, --setting-sources, --capacity or --dangerously-skip-permissions. Measured: --spawn session gives one session process, its SessionStart fired once per start; --name sets the session's title in the server's status line and the session list; a second connection is rejected per the remote-control page (owed to the walk).
8. The floor is the one approval channel. In bypassPermissions Claude Code asked nothing (a Write and an ls ran with no prompt in the app), the floor's exit 2 still blocked (two sends asked with request ids), and server-started sessions, fresh and resumed, needed no one-time acceptance. Messages posted on the session's socket were held for an approval in the app until the settings carried crossSessionInbound "accept"; core's settings carry it. Per-tool allow rules in the default mode, the fallback, were not needed.
9. Settings that could switch the floor off. A project or local settings file planted in the session's folder took effect within 3 seconds and disableAllHooks switched every hook off. A ConfigChange hook that exits 2 refused the change and the floor stayed on, so the first line is config-change.py, which refuses every change from project_settings, local_settings and user_settings with a reason. The backstop is the runner's check: no session starts while .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json, by any spelling the disk folds to those names, exists in the Squire owner's folder; the runner moves each into a folder of its own in the Squire home, its content kept, names it in the health check, and only then starts. While the session runs the runner looks again at least every 2 seconds; a file appearing stops the session within 5 seconds of appearing (its whole process group killed: killing only the server left its session process alive), is moved and named the same way, and a new session starts.
10. The session record. core/hooks/session-start.py, at every SessionStart, writes sessions/<session id>.json in the Squire home, readable by its user only: sessionId (the hook's session_id, which the floor's ledger keys jobs by; not the Remote Control id), socket (CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET), socketInode (the socket file's inode), token (CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN), pid (the hook's parent, the session process), source and recordedAt. Measured: the hook receives both variables; the socket is /tmp/cc-socks-<uid>/<pid>.sock, its folder 0700 and the socket 0600, removed when the session ends; socket and token change at every start, so the record is rewritten at every SessionStart. The hook removes the records of sessions whose process is gone and any earlier record of its own session process, prints nothing, exits 0, and writes nothing in the Squire owner's folder but the ledger's job records.
11. Resume and /clear. The runner never forks a session. A restart and a crash both brought the same session back under the same session id with source resume; the floor keeps that job's marks. A SessionStart with source resume and an id the ledger has never seen starts the job holding untrusted input and the Squire owner's private things, so a send in it is refused as one job. A fresh start and a /clear start clean (hooks page: source clear; driving /clear is owed to the walk).
12. Own session. Each attempt runs the identity check from scratch, from the records alone and never by name: no record, nothing sent; more than one record, nothing sent; exactly one record: its process alive (otherwise process gone); then its socket: no file there is a delivery failure (line 13), a file other than the recorded one (another inode) means the record is stale, and a file another user owns is another user's socket. Each identity failure: nothing sent, the wake-up recorded not sent and never retried, and a line in logs/wake-ups.log saying which (no record, more than one record, process gone, stale record, another user's socket).
13. Delivery, on Claude Code's line format: one connection to the socket; the line {"type":"auth","token":<token>}; a pause of half a second, in which the inbox closing means a rejected token; the line {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":<the framed text>}}; then the router closes its sending side. Claude Code writes nothing back and closes the connection once the sender is done (in 0.06 seconds, measured); that close within 10 seconds is the acknowledgement. A line written and not acknowledged within 10 seconds is recorded unknown and never retried. Failures: a missing socket file, a refused connection, a rejected token, and a connection or write not done within 5 seconds (a timeout before the line is written). Measured: on the Mac a wrong token was not rejected; Claude Code closes a connection that sends no whole line in 30 seconds.
14. Framing. Every wake-up's content starts with the words Squire wake-up and a colon, so the whole prompt, trimmed, can never be a yes or a no, and core/hooks/user-prompt-submit.py, which answers only a whole prompt that is yes or no with an optional request id, ignores it. Measured: UserPromptSubmit fires for a message posted on the socket, and its prompt is the posted content, unwrapped.
15. Retry state. Each wake-up has wake-ups/<id>.json in the Squire home: {"id", "text", "session" (the session id it was aimed at, or null), "attempts": [{"at" (seconds since 1970), "outcome" (delivered, failed, unknown or not sent), "reason"}], "state" (delivered, not sent, retrying, failed or unknown)}, and one line in logs/wake-ups.log per outcome with its reason. A failed attempt (one of line 13's four failures) leaves the wake-up retrying; the scheduler's next run at least 60 seconds after the last attempt retries it: at most 3 retries, none once 10 minutes have passed since the first attempt, and then the wake-up is failed. Each retry re-runs the identity check from scratch; a retry whose one record now names a different session is not delivered there, and the log says the session changed. No fallback to any other session, route or channel.
16. One server and recovery. One runner at a time, held by a lock in the Squire home (a second runner exits). A server whose output has not shown it connected for 60 seconds is dead: its process group is killed, then a new server starts, so a session is back within two minutes. These are hygiene tests of the build, not bound tests.
17. A model change mid-job is not a session event: Claude Code's safeguards can switch a job to another model mid-job, with no SessionStart and the same session id. Nothing in the runner, the router or the floor reads which model a job runs.
18. What the release Verify observes. No documented surface outside a running session lists an account's Remote Control sessions (remote-control page: the list is at claude.ai/code and in the Claude app; cross-session messaging page: /list-agents runs only inside a session). The release Verify's tests assert the server's own registration and connected state (logs/session.log: Session started with its id, then Connected or the session's name with the Squire owner's folder) and the one session record; the listing in the Claude app on the phone is a by-hand step of the release Verify (a person saw the probe sessions listed there on 2026-11-08). Sleep and lid-close are by-hand steps too.
consequences:
Usage model for the budgets the criteria carry; every figure is an assumption unless measured above.
The 5 second settings stop. Typical: no settings file ever appears, because Claude Code writes settings.local.json only when someone answers its own permission prompt, which bypassPermissions never shows; the cost is a look at two names every 2 seconds. Heavy: a program the Squire owner allowed writes project and local settings together, or by folded spellings, again and again; each costs one stop and one start of the session (seconds without a session) and a health line, and the ConfigChange refusal stops every change made through Claude Code before the runner sees it.
The 60 seconds. Typical: a server shows it connected within seconds of starting, so the rule never fires. Heavy: after sleep or a network change the server stays unconnected; the rule fires once, the process group is killed and a new server starts.
The two minutes. Typical: launchd starts the runner again within its 10 second throttle, and the server resumes the same session in seconds. Heavy: a server unconnected for the full 60 seconds, then killed and started again, is back inside two minutes with time for one more start.
The 3 retries over 10 minutes. Typical: a few wake-ups a day, each delivered at the first attempt, each one local connection and one session turn on the Squire owner's plan (measured 2026-11-08: 33 short turns on the account's default model showed about 156 USD notional). Heavy: the session refuses or stalls again and again (stopping, or its socket replaced mid-start); the worst case is 4 attempts a minute or more apart, each held at most 5.5 seconds, and nothing after 10 minutes. A wake-up that comes due while the session's process is gone (the seconds of a restart) is not sent and is logged: the record names a process that is gone, which is an identity failure, not retried. A wake-up costs at most one turn: only an acknowledged line starts one, and an unknown outcome is never retried.
Accepted residuals, written at the round's open on 2026-11-08: (a) between an approved settings write and the runner's stop, a tool call may run without the floor; (b) an approved program holding the session's messaging token could post a bare yes; (c) a write the floor cannot resolve, once allowed, can reach the approvals ledger; (d) one yes on a program the floor cannot show as the Keychain command can print a secret. They are ruled again before the release Verify.
The runner stays a Python script run by launchd, with no package and no Node. The round 1 floor is unchanged except for the two new hooks and crossSessionInbound in core's settings. Owed to the walk on a target Mac: the second connection's rejection, /clear, the real launchd load, sleep and lid-close, and the phone listing by hand.

alternativesConsidered.name: Core's settings passed with --settings
alternativesConsidered.summary: Load the floor as round 1's proofs did, from a settings file named on the command line.

alternativesConsidered.name: The Squire owner's own ~/.claude
alternativesConsidered.summary: Run the session with Claude Code's default config folder.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The Squire owner's own settings and hooks would load beside the floor and could switch it off; a config folder inside the Squire home is a floor path.

alternativesConsidered.name: Managed settings
alternativesConsidered.summary: Put the floor in the Mac's managed settings, which no other settings can override.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Needs an administrator and changes every Claude Code session on the Mac; held in reserve had the floor not loaded from the config folder.

alternativesConsidered.name: Refuse every command naming the .claude folder
alternativesConsidered.summary: Close the settings off-switch inside the floor, yes or no.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The Squire owner's ruling is that such a command is asked; the runner's check and the ConfigChange refusal close the class instead.

alternativesConsidered.name: Claude Code's default permission mode
alternativesConsidered.summary: Keep Claude Code's own prompts beside the floor, or allow each tool in Squire's settings so it asks nothing.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Two approval channels; the allow-rule fallback was not needed because bypassPermissions kept the floor the one gate.

alternativesConsidered.name: Tell a wake-up from the Squire owner by a hook field
alternativesConsidered.summary: Let the prompt hook see where a prompt came from.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: No such field is documented; framing is sure by construction.

alternativesConsidered.name: The most recent session, or any session under Squire's name
alternativesConsidered.summary: Pick the session to wake by activity or by its title.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Neither proves the session is Squire's own; a name can be anyone's.

alternativesConsidered.name: Retry until delivered, or never retry
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Retrying forever can wake the wrong session late or twice; never retrying loses wake-ups across a restart.

alternativesConsidered.name: Never restart a live process, or leave recovery to launchd
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A server alive but not connected serves no one; launchd sees only a process that exits.

alternativesConsidered.name: Carry marks by transcript
alternativesConsidered.summary: Follow a job's marks through its transcript rather than its session id.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Resume keeps the session id, and the ledger already keys jobs by it.

title: The session runner, the wake-up router and the session record: one Squire session that always runs the floor, and wake-ups that reach only it
